name: Clementine
short_status: Mapped the whole Moon Feb 26 to Apr 22, 1994 (297 orbits, about 1.6 million images); left lunar orbit May 3, 1994; a thruster fault on May 7 ended the Geographos flyby plan; mission terminated Aug 8, 1994.
tagline: BMDO and NASA · United States · Orbiter · 1994 · The quiet decades Partial
stats: digital images returned in two months of lunar mapping
lunar orbits flown between February 19 and May 3, 1994
since the previous US Moon mission (Explorer 49, 1973)
build cost; NRL completed the spacecraft in 22 months

facts.label: Program
facts.value: Deep Space Program Science Experiment (DSPSE); a technology proving mission for the Strategic Defense Initiative's Brilliant Pebbles concept, managed jointly by the Ballistic Missile Defense Organization and NASA

facts.label: Builder
facts.value: US Naval Research Laboratory, which completed the spacecraft in 22 months for less than $80 million and flight-tested 23 advanced lightweight technologies (NRL figures)

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 25 January 1994, 16:34 UT, on a Titan 2G (vehicle 23G-11) from Vandenberg Air Force Base SLC-4W, California

facts.label: Return to the Moon
facts.value: First US mission to the Moon in 21 years; the previous one was the Explorer 49 radio astronomy orbiter, launched June 1973

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 227 kg dry, 424 kg with propellant; total launch mass 1,690 kg, most of it the solid rocket motor for translunar injection

facts.label: Sensors
facts.value: UV/Visible camera, near-infrared camera, long-wave infrared camera, high-resolution camera, two star tracker cameras, LIDAR laser altimeter, and a charged particle telescope

facts.label: Lunar orbit insertion
facts.value: 19 February 1994, into an elliptical polar orbit of roughly 430 x 2,950 km

facts.label: Mapping output
facts.value: About 1.6 million digital images over two months, many at resolutions of 100-200 m, giving scientists their first look at the total lunar landscape including the polar regions; 297 lunar orbits in all

facts.label: Topography
facts.value: The laser altimeter profiled the South Pole-Aitken Basin as a topographic rim about 2,500 km in diameter with an irregular depressed floor about 12 km deep

facts.label: Bistatic radar result
facts.value: A same-sense circular polarization enhancement localized to the permanently shadowed south polar region and absent from periodically sunlit terrain, including the north pole; the probable explanation offered was low-loss volume scattering by deposits such as water ice (Nozette et al., Science, 29 Nov 1996)

facts.label: Ice announcement
facts.value: 3 December 1996: Department of Defense officials announced evidence of ice in the bottom of a permanently shadowed south pole crater, estimated at 60,000 to 120,000 cubic meters

facts.label: The counter-evidence
facts.value: Arecibo radar observations published in 2006 (Campbell et al., Nature) found the same radar signatures in sunlit terrain where ice cannot survive, concluding there was no evidence for thick ice deposits near the south pole; surface roughness explains the signal equally well

timeline: Launched at 16:34 UT on a Titan 2G from Vandenberg Air Force Base, the first US spacecraft sent to the Moon in over 20 years
Entered an elliptical polar lunar orbit of about 430 x 2,950 km after phasing orbits and an Earth flyby
Systematic mapping begins from a five-hour polar orbit
Bistatic radar pass: the spacecraft beams its 13-cm radio signal onto the shadowed south polar terrain while Deep Space Network antennas on Earth listen for the echo
Mapping campaign complete: the entire lunar surface imaged, including the first good look at both poles
Thrusters fire to leave lunar orbit, targeting an August 1994 flyby of near-Earth asteroid 1620 Geographos via an Earth flyby
A computer fault at 14:39 UT fires an attitude control thruster for 11 minutes, exhausting the propellant and leaving the spacecraft in an uncontrollable spin; the asteroid flyby is abandoned
Lunar gravity takes control of the crippled spacecraft and propels it into heliocentric orbit
Mission terminated when falling power levels no longer allow clear telemetry exchange
20 Feb to 10 May 1995
Ground controllers briefly regain contact after the derelict fortuitously drifts into an attitude that lets it power up
Nozette and colleagues publish the bistatic radar experiment in Science, reporting a polarization signature over the shadowed south pole consistent with water ice
The Department of Defense announces evidence of ice in a permanently shadowed crater at the lunar south pole

A Stanford reanalysis of the raw bistatic echoes cannot confirm an enhancement unique to the south pole; meanwhile Lunar Prospector's neutron spectrometer independently finds hydrogen at both poles in March 1998

Arecibo observations published in Nature find identical radar signatures in sunlit terrain, concluding there is no evidence for thick polar ice deposits; Clementine's specific radar claim remains contested
